positions.commentary: The speaker suggested that Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger may have had second thoughts about IBM after talking to lower-level employees.

thesis: This episode argues that IBM is a bearish investment due to internal dysfunction, including a toxic culture where lower-level employees openly criticized leadership and the company was losing talent to Apple. The speaker highlights a lack of execution on new ideas, a CEO admitting that 10-15% of employees lack necessary technical skills, and suggests that even major investors like Buffett and Munger may have reconsidered their position after hearing these internal issues.

claims.claim: The speaker missed IBM because lower-level employees gave unprintable negative reviews of the CEO and Chairman, and the company was losing talent to Apple.
claims.quote: We gave IBM a miss. We didn't short it because we don't like shorting. We shot only very few stocks. And also it has dividends. So it's a barter.

claims.claim: IBM employees complained that the company had many new ideas but nobody executed on them, and bringing Apple R&D people in would be like bringing a fox into a henhouse.
claims.quote: IBM people complained they have a lot of new ideas, nobody executes on them. If you're going to bring the Fox, you're going to bring the fox into the henhouse to steal more ideas, not only you don't trust them, but it shows poor judgment.

claims.claim: The CEO publicly admitted that 10 or 15 percent of IBM employees did not keep up their technical skills and would be let go if they did not catch up.
claims.quote: Now, within a few months after that, the CEO said fairly publicly that about 10 or 15 percent of IBM employees didn't keep up their technical skills. And she's going to let them, like, one or two years to catch up.

claims.claim: The speaker suggested that Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger may have had second thoughts about IBM after talking to lower-level employees.
claims.quote: So I believe that if Warren Buffett and Charlie Mangier, who are certainly smarter than me, if they have talked to people at IBM lower level, I would suggest they may have had second thoughts.
